t: Check If It Is a Good Array — Bézout's Identity and the GCD Trick
o:
We may pick any subset of `nums`, multiply each chosen element by *any* integer (positive, negative, or zero), and ask whether some combination sums to exactly 1. This is precisely asking whether 1 lies in the set of all integer linear combinations of the array elements. By **Bézout's identity**, the set of all integer combinations of numbers $a_1,\dots,a_n$ is exactly the set of multiples of $g = \gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n)$. So the answer is simply: is the GCD of the whole array equal to 1?

**Example 1:** [12,5,7,23] → gcd(12,5)=1, so overall gcd = 1 → true (indeed 5·3 + 7·(−2) = 1).

**Example 2:** [29,6,10] → gcd(29,6)=1 → gcd = 1 → true.

**Example 3:** [3,6] → gcd = 3; every combination is a multiple of 3, never 1 → false.

With n up to 10^5 and values up to 10^9, we need an O(n log(max)) single pass — brute-force search over subsets/multipliers is exponential and hopeless.
k: A sum of integer multiples of array elements can equal 1 iff the GCD of all elements is 1 (Bézout's identity).
The GCD of an array is computed by folding pairwise gcds in one pass.
Any common divisor d > 1 divides every achievable sum, so gcd > 1 immediately means 'not good'.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force over small subsets (conceptual)
a.i: Try pairs/triples of elements and check whether their integer combination can produce 1 using the extended Euclidean algorithm on each pair. For two numbers a, b, ax + by = g has solutions for x, y, so a pair works iff gcd(a,b)=1. Checking only pairs fails in general (e.g., [6,10,15]: every pair has gcd > 1 but gcd(6,10,15)=1), so you'd need to extend to triples — exponential blow-up. Included mainly to motivate why a global invariant (the GCD) is the right tool.
s: For every pair (a,b), run extended Euclid to get gcd(a,b).
If any pair has gcd 1, return true.
Otherwise try triples via extended Euclid on (gcd(a,b), c); this grows combinatorially.
This does not scale — abandon it.
a.t: O(n^2 log(max)) — all pairs, each gcd costs logarithmic time. Too slow for n = 10^5 and incorrect for cases like [6,10,15].
a.sp: O(1) extra space (ignoring recursion stack of Euclid).

a.n: Approach 2: Fold the GCD of the whole array (optimal)
a.i: By Bézout's identity, integers $x_1,\dots,x_n$ with $\sum x_i a_i = 1$ exist iff $\gcd(a_1,\dots,a_n) = 1$. Necessity: any common divisor divides the sum. Sufficiency: repeatedly combine two elements into their gcd (which is itself an integer combination of them), shrinking the set until one number remains — that number is the total gcd, and it's reachable as a combination; if it equals 1 we're done. So just compute the running GCD in one pass.
s: For each num, set g = gcd(g, num).
a.t: O(n log M) where M = max(nums) — one gcd per element, each O(log M) arithmetic steps.

w: In an interview, state Bézout's identity first, then implement the one-pass GCD fold — Approach 2 is the expected answer; skip the brute force except as a discussion point about why local checks fail ([6,10,15] is the killer counterexample). Pitfalls: forgetting that multipliers may be negative (this is what makes Bézout applicable), initializing the fold with 0 rather than nums[0] (both work since gcd(0,x)=x), and assuming all-positive inputs restrict anything — signs don't matter for gcd. Edge cases: single-element arrays are good iff the element is 1; arrays like [2,4,6] are never good. Follow-ups: reconstruct the actual coefficients with the extended Euclidean algorithm, or handle the variant asking for a target sum t (answer: t must be a multiple of the array gcd).
